places.name: Thính Vũ Lâu
places.size: A great sect's old founding seat on a dormant volcanic cone: a domain about 6 km across with hundreds of buildings (about 250), now much quieter since the court moved away in 1166-1170: the first elder, a few dozen disciples and a thousand servants, artisans and mortal families remain; the Rain Tower on the crown is kept.
places.where: Volcano, 2.19 km up, inland, rain forest all round. Fire qi dominates (53 %), no Thunder. Ma đạo great sect, tier 1. Nearest: the peak Lâm Linh Đỉnh 75 km, the ruin Hạ Lôi Thành 90 km. Its lamps have never been lit since the Night Rain Edict. Map crop: a black volcanic cone with a small crater in the middle of rolling green and grassy hills, a river looping around its western foot, bare grey crags to the north, a small blue lake at its south-western foot, rain forest to the south; no sea in view. Per the sect pages it is now the OLD seat (the court moved to Thần Cổ Phong in 1166-1170) and the tower stays as the Rain Tower under the first elder.
places.imagined: A downpour at dusk. Every eave of the slender tower runs with water through bronze rain-chains and the whole tower rings like a struck bell, with no lamp in any window.
places.subject: The place: Thính Vũ Lâu, the Tower of Listening to the Rain, seen from above, in heavy rain. Setting: a dormant volcanic cone about six kilometres across rising out of rolling green hills and rain forest, a river looping around its western foot, bare grey crags to the north and a small blue lake at its south-western foot, its flanks terraced with banana groves in glossy green, a crater lake of grey water at the crown, great banks of storm cloud hanging low and grey sheets of rain crossing the forest all round. The sect's domain covers the whole cone: about two hundred and fifty buildings in dark timber and black tile on terraces that ring the cone in broad spirals, long covered galleries, drum and bell towers, round dormitory halls, training yards of black stone, soul-vault entrances cut into the rock, and roads climbing in switchbacks from the forest, with banana groves below them. On the crown stands the founder's tower: a slender many-eaved pagoda of twenty-one storeys, the tallest thing in the south, taller than the cone's crater walls. From every eave of every storey hang long bronze rain-chains, hundreds of them, so that in the downpour the whole tower runs with silver water and ranges of white streams pour down its sides into catch-basins. No lamp burns in any window of the tower or the halls; the whole domain is dark. Mortal families and servants are tiny figures sheltering in the lower terraces under oiled-paper umbrellas; only about a third of the halls show any life. Dim grey-violet light, a thin gold gleam from the upper left. Since the court left, the upper terraces are shuttered: the broad training yards are empty, rain pools in their hollows, and creepers have begun to climb the black gate towers, while the first elder's few dozen disciples keep a single hall and the tower alive. Water from the crater lake runs in a spiral gutter down the cone, so that one silver thread winds from the tower's foot to the river.

places.name: Hồng Đậu Trang
places.size: A minor sect's manor, now the gracious door after the sect moved into its spirit vein: about 40 members (mostly women) and gardeners, a walled manor of three terraces about 250 m across with about 40 buildings.
places.where: Jungle at 40 m on the coast where rain forest meets the sea. Water qi. Ma đạo minor sect, vassal of Thính Vũ Lâu, founded 910. Nearest: the ruin Lan Tân Trấn 106 km, the spirit vein Tiêu Âm Mạch 135 km. Map crop: a rocky green coast on the north shore of a blue bay, forested hills behind, a small lake to the north-west and a river to the north-east. Per the sect pages this is the old seat, kept as 'the gracious door' (the sect's cultivators moved to Tiêu Âm Mạch).
places.imagined: Afternoon, humid. A perfect round moon gate of red lacquer wreathed in scarlet black-eyed beans, a path of crushed shell.
places.subject: The place: Hồng Đậu Trang, the Manor of Red Beans, seen from above where rain forest meets the sea. Setting: glossy dark-green jungle on all sides, a pale curve of beach and a calm blue-green sea at one edge, thin mist among the trees. Since the sect moved inland the manor stands as the gracious door, still receiving guests, on three terraces, a walled compound about two hundred and fifty metres across with a whitewashed wall and red-lacquered gate buildings, about forty buildings in all: red-lacquered halls with dark glazed roofs rising step by step, long covered corridors, a lantern pavilion, guest courtyards with tea tables, a large walled garden of poisonous and fragrant plants in beautiful patterned beds, and a still lily pond. The whole manor is half buried in glossy leaves, vines spilling over the roofs. Its entrance is a perfect round moon gate of red lacquer in the front wall, so thickly wreathed in vines of scarlet, black-eyed beans that the lacquer barely shows, with a path of crushed white shell leading to it from the forest road, where a small party of guests arrives with a palanquin. Women in red and black robes, about a dozen, walk the corridors and tend the garden, tiny figures, while the upper terraces stand quiet, shuttered, and swept. A faint pink-gold haze lies over the garden. Golden light from the upper left, soft long shadows. The garden's centre is a round pond with a nine-arched stone bridge, and the beds are laid in the pattern of an open fan, red-beaned creepers above and pale glossy leaves below. Eight guest houses stand along the shore terrace with lacquered doors and tea tables set under awnings. A path of crushed white shell runs down a long stair to a small harbour where two coasting vessels lie, and the surf behind the cove is white against black volcanic rock.

places.name: Thu Trì Thành
places.size: A walled port city built in steps up wooded hills: about 3 km across, some 25,000 roofs and about 110,000 people, with tiers of square stone pools descending through its streets and the Night Rain Market on the lower terraces.
places.where: Grassland at sea level where a river meets the sea below wooded hills. Water qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu, founded 400. Home of the Night Rain Market of ma đạo pills and poisons. Nearest: the hot spring Quế Hương Thang 177 km. Map crop: a river mouth on the north shore of a blue bay, wooded hills behind, a small stream and green slopes at the left; forest pockets stand further inland to the west.
places.imagined: After night rain: every pool brimming and spilling into the next, the whole city murmuring, dark oiled-paper awnings over the lower market.
places.subject: The place: Thu Trì Thành, Autumn Pools City, seen from above at dusk after rain. Setting: wooded hills rising at the back in dark green, a river mouth with a wide muddy-brown estuary, a grey sea, and low rain clouds with a thin gold gap at the horizon. The city is built in steps down a slope to the harbour, a walled port about three kilometres across, with a grey-brick wall with fourteen gate towers, a faint shimmer of the guardian array over the wall. Tiers of square stone pools, some thirty, descend through the streets from the upper town to the harbour like a staircase of mirrors, each about twenty metres across, edged in white stone, brimming and spilling over small lips into the next, with ribbons of water shining down the whole slope. Between them lie about twenty-five thousand grey and black tile roofs in dense lanes, temples with dark red roofs, bridges, and canals. Over the lower terraces hang the dark oiled-paper awnings of the Night Rain Market: a sea of overlapping black-brown canopies about four hundred metres across, with lantern light glowing through the paper in dim red and gold, crowds under it, and a few cloaked figures. The harbour holds fifty ships. Tiny umbrellas move along the streets. Light from the upper left, lamp-glow in the shadows. The Night Rain Market's awnings are held by about two hundred tall poles with coloured cord, and below them the lanes are barely a shoulder wide. A dozen pill-sellers' booths each have a single lantern of a different colour. Along the pools, stepping-stone paths cross every second basin, and children float paper boats down the cascade. Rainwater is gathered from every roof into the pools by a hundred gutters, and a large canal along the east wall carries the overflow to the harbour.

places.name: Bình Dã Trấn
places.size: A walled drying town of about 1,200 roofs and 5,000 people, wall about 800 m across, centred on a paved brick yard about 250 m square.
places.where: Grassland at 90 m on a river, on the one open plain in the south where it rarely rains. Wood qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the beast lair Mãng Đằng Lâm 79 km, the village Kiều Bạn 150 km. Map crop: a braided river with several channels running through green hills, with golden grass and some forest; the town is at a river junction where a stream joins from the north and south.
places.imagined: A dry day. The great sun-baked brick yard is covered edge to edge with mats of drying tea, herbs, cloth and grain.
places.subject: The place: Bình Dã Trấn, Level Plain Town, seen from above an open plain cleared from rain forest. Setting: an open green-gold plain among rolling hills, with dark wet rain forest all along its edge in a wall of green and a braided river of several silver channels winding through, joined by streams from north and south, a sunny sky. The town is a walled square about eight hundred metres across with a grey-brick wall, four gates and corner towers, about twelve hundred grey-tile roofs, and at its centre a huge paved yard of sun-baked red brick about two hundred and fifty metres square, with the grey roofs gathered around it. The yard is covered edge to edge with thousands of mats in patterns: green mats of drying tea, yellow and brown mats of herbs, bright bolts of cloth in blues and reds laid out flat, and pale grain in pools and squares, so that the yard looks like a patchwork of coloured squares. Outside the east gate a long line of porters and ox-carts from the forest, carrying wet harvests in baskets, waits to enter, and townsfolk with long rakes turn the mats, tiny figures. Strong sun from the upper left, hard short shadows lengthening to the lower right, hazy distance. Each mat is two metres by one, and the yard's centre holds a raised stone platform with a weighing beam where the town's fee-clerks stand. Rope barriers divide the yard into twelve lots, each marked by a pole with a coloured cloth. A gong tower forty metres tall rises at one corner of the yard. At the river's edge the town's three wooden bridges are packed with carts and porters, and boats ferry baskets across from the forest bank. A cloud of steam rises from the tea-curing shed, and a row of men with bamboo rakes turns the herbs.

places.name: Xuân Thảo Thành
places.size: A walled river city of about 18,000 roofs and 80,000 people, with thick turf-capped earthen walls about 2.5 km across.
places.where: Grassland at 40 m on a river at the forest's edge. Wood qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu, founded 640 on land given after the Petal Shore fighting. Nearest: the forest Thanh Hoàng Lâm 75 km, the hot spring Ôn Vũ Thang 190 km. Map crop: a river junction on rolling green-gold hills with forest pockets, a blue lake or bay to the north-east, and low forest to the south-west.
places.imagined: Spring turf-cutting day: the whole city is out recutting and replanting the turf on the walls, a festival.
places.subject: The place: Xuân Thảo Thành, Spring Grass City, seen from above at the edge of a forest in spring. Setting: a river running along the edge of a great forest in dark green, open meadows of fresh grass in the foreground, with old blackened tree stumps scattered in the meadows, grown over with grass and flowers. The city is enclosed by thick earthen walls about two and a half kilometres across, twelve metres thick at their base, whose tops are capped with living turf, bright green even in the dry months, with gate towers of timber and tile. Inside are about eighteen thousand grey-tile roofs standing among young trees, in lanes and courtyards, with a river canal, a market square, bridges, and a large temple of the grass with a green roof. Along the top of the walls, in a line a couple of kilometres long, thousands of citizens are recutting and replanting turf in long strips, with rolls of turf piled on carts and long rows of figures with spades, children, flags of coloured cloth being the only decoration, bright green stripes of new turf against older darker green. Outside the walls the charred stumps stay untouched in the meadows, and a path winds between them. Fresh spring light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. The wall's turf is cut in strips a metre wide and laid on a lattice of bamboo. At the east gate a bridge of three arches carries the road over the river, and a long wharf holds timber rafts. Inside, two broad avenues cross at a stone drum tower, and the temple of the grass has a roof tiled in green. The festival is led by a dais of twelve elders with long rakes; behind them stand wheelbarrows of turf in rows of fifty, each with a name painted on it.

places.name: Kiều Bạn Thôn
places.size: A bridge village of about 30 houses and an inn, 130 people, at one end of a roofed timber bridge about 60 m long.
places.where: Grassland at 10 m where the forest road crosses a slow river. Wood qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the town Bình Dã 150 km, the town Liễu Ngạn 177 km. Map crop: a braided river of several channels winding through green hills with golden grass and pockets of forest; a bridge-village at one of the river's bends.
places.imagined: Dusk. Rows of worn straw sandals hung under the deep eaves of the bridge.
places.subject: The place: Kiều Bạn Thôn, Bridge Companion Village, seen from above a slow river in the forest. Setting: a wide, quiet green river flowing through a grassy meadow bordered by rain forest, a forest road arriving from the south and leaving to the north. A roofed timber bridge about sixty metres long, with a long gabled roof with deep eaves, spans the river on stout piers. Under the eaves of the bridge hang long rows of worn straw sandals, hundreds of them, pale gold on dark timber. At the bridge's northern end a cluster of about thirty grey-tile houses crowds the road, with a two-storey inn with a veranda and a courtyard full of travellers' carts, a stall selling new sandals, stables, a shrine, and small gardens. At the southern end a stack of old sandals stands piled on the bank, ready for the annual burning. Travellers cross, some barefoot, a merchant with a mule train, a monk, tiny figures; a woman at the stall fits a sandal to a traveller. Smoke from kitchens rises into a violet dusk, lanterns lit on the bridge beams. Soft golden light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. The bridge has a roof of dark shingle, thirty-two posts painted red on each side, and benches along the inside. The sandals are hung on cords from the beams, in rows about twelve deep, and a thousand pairs of straw sandals stir slightly in the draught. The inn has forty beds in a long upstairs gallery and a courtyard well. At the northern end a covered market of eight stalls sells sandals, tea eggs, medicine and oil lamps. A carter checks a wheel while two porters argue over a sandal.

places.name: Bình Độ Thôn
places.size: A ferry village of about 35 houses and 150 people on a wide, glassy river with one great flat raft ferry.
places.where: Grassland at 100 m on a wide, slow forest river. Wood qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the forest Long Nhãn Lâm 112 km, the village Hoa Điền 158 km. Map crop: a thin river meandering through rolling green forest-hills and golden grass, with a bay of the sea at the right edge about a hundred kilometres away; the ferry is at a bend where a stream joins.
places.imagined: A noon so calm the river is glass; a raft with a thatched sleeping shelter poled across, passengers asleep.
places.subject: The place: Bình Độ Thôn, Calm Crossing Village, seen from above a wide forest river. Setting: a broad, slow river about four hundred metres wide, so glassy that it reflects the sky and the forest on both banks perfectly, with dark green rain forest in tall walls along both shores and a low mist. On the near bank sits a village of about thirty-five grey-tile houses with a ferry landing: a sloping stone slipway, a wooden pier, a ferry-house with a bell that is never rung, boat sheds, drying nets, and a small tea house. A broad flat raft, twelve metres long, with a small thatched sleeping shelter on its deck, is poled across the river by two ferrymen in silence, with a few passengers asleep on mats in the shelter; the wake behind it is a faint thin V in the glass. Two other rafts wait at the landing. On the far bank a small landing and a road enter the forest. Nobody shouts and nothing disturbs the water: the village has no drum. A lone fisherman sits in a boat. Soft light from the upper left, slow mist in the trees, long shadows to the lower right. The raft is built of eight great logs lashed together, and its sleeping shelter has a roof of rice-straw and sides of woven mats, with a lamp hanging at the stern. Four ferrymen, each with a long pole, pass it in silence, and a passenger sleeps with his head on a sack. The village's boat-sheds house ten rafts, and the only sound is the cry of a heron. A tea-house on the bank has six mats and a kettle on a charcoal stove, with a cup laid out at the foot of every mat for the sleepers' waking.

places.name: Hoa Điền Thôn
places.size: A flower village of about 40 houses and 180 people among about 60 hectares of flower fields in long strips, with a wall of about 300 beehives.
places.where: Grassland at 70 m on a river. Wood qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the hot spring Ôn Vũ Thang 79 km, the forest Thanh Hoàng Lâm 125 km. Map crop: a thin river with side streams winding through rolling green hills and forest pockets, a small bay of the sea at the east edge about a hundred kilometres away.
places.imagined: Midsummer. Sweeping strips of purple, yellow and white flowers, a hum of bees.
places.subject: The place: Hoa Điền Thôn, Flower Field Village, seen from above in midsummer. Setting: a river meandering through low green country, rain forest dark along the horizon, and a sky of high thin cloud. Sweeping fields of flowers cover the floodplain in long curving strips about sixty hectares in all, in bands of purple, yellow and white, each strip a hundred metres wide and a kilometre long, so the plain looks like a great striped cloth, with narrow grassy paths between. Along the village's edge runs a wall of stacked hollow-log beehives, about three hundred, in rows three and four high, with a haze of bees visible above, a smoke curl from a beekeeper's pot. The village is about forty grey-tile houses with yards, honey-pressing sheds with long tables, jar stores, and a small shrine, along a lane beside the river, with a landing where honey jars are loaded on boats for the south. Beekeepers in white veils, a few dozen tiny figures, work the hives and talk to them; flower pickers walk the strips with baskets; children chase butterflies. Warm bright light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. Twelve pickers' paths run between the strips, and each strip is a different crop: lavender-purple clover, yellow rapeseed, white buckwheat, pink vetch. A honey-press house with a long tiled roof stands at the river end, and the jar store holds about two thousand stoneware jars in stacks. The hives are of split log with a clay lid and a painted number; the beekeepers sit on low stools by the hive wall and speak softly to the bees. A bridge of planks crosses to the village's second flower-field, with a young girl bringing the news to the hives.

places.name: Yên Kiều Thôn
places.size: A village of about 30 houses and 130 people at one end of a long stone slab bridge about 500 m long on many low piers.
places.where: Low meadows at 50 m on a river. Wood qi. Holder Hồng Đậu Trang. Nearest: the forest Tân Lang Lâm 75 km, the forest Dung Thụ Lâm 230 km. Map crop: a river through low meadows with forest pockets, thin fog over it, and the sea at the lower-left corner; faint bare rock at the lower right.
places.imagined: Rain and mist: the long bridge fading into fog before it reaches the far bank.
places.subject: The place: Yên Kiều Thôn, Misty Bridge Village, seen from above in rain and mist. Setting: low green meadows and reed beds along a wide misty river about three hundred metres wide, grey water, pale fog hanging low and thick over the far half of the river and swallowing the far shore completely. A long narrow bridge of grey stone slabs on many low piers, about five hundred metres long, runs out from the village across the river, clear and sharp for the first third, then paler and paler until it fades into the fog and vanishes before reaching the other side; the line of piers shows only as a faint dotted line. At the near end sit about thirty grey-tile houses along the bank in two short rows with yards, a stone landing, a small ferry hut, a shrine with a bell, fish racks, and a few boats. Two figures cross the bridge holding a rope between them, tiny against the mist, with a third waiting at the start with a lantern. Rain streaks, wet stone gleaming, dim silver light from the upper left, soft long shadows. The bridge has seventy-four low stone piers, each one a metre wide, spaced three paces apart, and a waist-high rope rail strung between wooden posts. The slab road is only wide enough for two people side by side. The fog lies in bands; in one clear gap you can see the bridge's pale line, then the next piers in silhouette. A guide-stone with a bell stands at the start, and a villager rings it to count the steps. The houses are of grey stone with deep eaves, and a drying rack of rope stands at the landing.

places.name: Tàn Hà Hồ
places.size: A grey lake about 35 km long on the map at the foot of a volcanic cone, crowded with withered lotus; no buildings, a few mourners' benches on the shore.
places.where: A lake at 120 m, inland, beside Thính Vũ Lâu (230 km away across the map). Earth qi. No holder. Nearest: the lake Kính Thủy Đàm 90 km, the village Thảo Lư 103 km. The founder kept the withered lotus to listen to the rain. Map crop: a small blue lake about 35 km long on a bare grey-brown hillside, at the foot of a dark volcanic cone to the north-east and bare crags, with a rust-orange hill to the west and dense forest to the south.
places.imagined: Summer that looks like the end of autumn: tall brown stalks, curled dry leaves and empty seedpods never cut.
places.subject: The place: Tàn Hà Hồ, the Withered Lotus Lake, seen from above under a pewter sky. Setting: a grey lake about thirty-five kilometres long on a bare hillside at the foot of a dark volcanic cone with banana-green slopes, with grey crags behind, dense forest to the south, a low shore of grey stones, and thin rain falling. The whole surface of the lake is crowded with withered lotus: millions upon millions of tall brown stalks bent at the top, curled dry leaves the colour of old paper and tea, and empty round seedpods hanging like shower heads, so the lake looks russet and grey-brown like the end of autumn even though the forest around is summer green. Narrow channels of open grey water wind through the thicket, and a few pale gaps show the sky. Nothing is cut and nothing cleared. Along the shore at one point a row of about twenty small figures in dark robes sit cross-legged on flat stones facing the water with their eyes closed, listening to each drop falling on the dry leaves, with a couple of simple stone benches behind them. A faint line of rain moves over the water. One lone lotus in bloom pink at the edge, about to wither. Dim silver light from the upper left, soft long shadows. The lake is kept so by custom: not one stalk has been cut since the founder's day, and in the thickest part the stems stand shoulder to shoulder across a kilometre. A line of stepping-stones runs out a hundred metres into the thicket and ends at a flat stone seat where the sect's first elder sits listening in storms. Frogs and dragonflies have made a home of the dry leaves, and raindrops make a hissing patter that carries across the water.

places.name: Hắc Hùng Lĩnh
places.size: A forested highland ridge about 12 km long held by black bears; no buildings, only a woodcutters' cairn at the foot.
places.where: Highland at 1.06 km, inland, above the rain forest of Tiêu Vũ Lâm. Earth qi. No holder; beast bone resource. Nearest: the peak Thụy Ngưu Sơn 202 km, the ruin Phi Anh Quán 237 km. Map crop: a rust-red banded ridge of highland with snowy grey crags behind and forest and golden grass below; a small lake at the right edge. No sea in view.
places.imagined: A tilted grey slab scored with deep parallel claw marks at the mouth of a dark cave.
places.subject: The place: Hắc Hùng Lĩnh, the Black Bear Ridge, seen from above. Setting: a highland ridge about twelve kilometres long rising above rain forest, its slopes banded rust-red and grey with dark conifers and broadleaf trees clinging to the folds and broken by huge boulders and rock outcrops, snowy grey crags behind, mist in the hollows below and wisps of cloud on the crest. About two-thirds of the way up a rock face opens a dark cave mouth about ten metres wide, with a worn bare earth apron in front of it. At the mouth of the cave stands a tilted slab of grey rock, as tall as two men, scored with deep parallel claw marks in bundles of four and five, pale scars, the freshest ones almost white; around it the earth is trampled and bare and scattered with bones and chewed honey combs. Honey trees stand on the slope below, with broken branches and one huge black bear, tiny, reaching up into a tree. Two more bears move along a ridge path, dark small shapes with lighter muzzles. At the foot of the ridge, a cairn of stones with a few pieces of woodcutters' rope marks the limit of how far men will go, with two tiny woodcutters standing well back. Cold clear light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. Cub tracks, as small as a plate, cross the beaten earth in front of the cave, and the cave's roof is polished black by generations of shoulders. A raised rock ledge opposite serves as the den-master's lookout. Beehives in hollow trees along the ridge path are marked with claw-ripped bark, and the autumn berry fields on the lower slope are trampled flat. The woodcutters' cairn is shoulder-high, built of forty or fifty flat stones, each placed by a different hand.

places.name: Tiêu Âm Mạch
places.size: A spirit vein in jungle, now the sect's seat (the back garden): a hidden garden valley about 1 km across, about 30 buildings of a minor sect of about 40 members.
places.where: Jungle at 40 m, inland, three days by cart from the manor Hồng Đậu Trang. Wood qi. The sect moved here in the plan; the vein becomes a minor seat. Nearest: Hồng Đậu Trang 135 km, the ruin Lan Tân Trấn 135 km. Map crop: grass and forest hills well inland of a large blue sea inlet along the south-west edge; dark forest pockets, a river to the north-east. Per the sect pages this is the sect's present seat, moved from the manor Hồng Đậu Trang; the vein becomes the minor seat.
places.imagined: Dappled dusk. A secret garden in a jungle valley where the ground glows faintly green with the vein beneath.
places.subject: The place: Tiêu Âm Mạch, the Vein of Quiet Sound, the back garden of a sect of poisons and charms, seen from above a jungle valley. Setting: dense dark-green jungle and grass in rolling hills, a hidden valley about a kilometre across, rimmed on all sides by steep green walls and cloaked in thin mist, with a great blue bay of the sea far off at the south-west, with no road visible but a single narrow track entering through a cleft. In the valley, through the leaves, the ground glows faintly green along lines of the spirit vein, a network of luminous streaks like veins under skin, branching out across the valley floor and meeting at a bright pool in the middle. Around the pool is a lovely garden: terraces and beds of poisonous and fragrant plants in curved patterns with red, violet and black flowers, bridges over little streams, willows and a pavilion on stilts. About thirty buildings of dark timber and red-lacquered posts with green tile roofs are tucked among the trees: a main hall, a pavilion, long dormitories, drying sheds and greenhouses with glass roofs, all half hidden by leaves and hanging creepers. A dozen women in red and black robes tend the beds, tiny figures. The mist and the green glow lend a dreamlike quiet. Dappled gold light from the upper left through the canopy, long shadows. The sect's present dormitory is a long house on stilts with sixteen rooms and a veranda, and the hall of the new seat stands over the central pool on piles. Poison beds are fenced in low bamboo hurdles marked by coloured threads; the red ones are never touched. Two glass-roofed greenhouses hold seedlings, and charm-strings hang from every branch of the willows, tinkling faintly. A narrow path along the cleft is the only way in and is watched by a single sleepy gate-keeper in a bamboo hut.
